<STRUCT_0001>
A solid treatment of quasi-finite morphisms is the basis of many developments
further down the road. It will lead to various versions of Zariski's Main
Theorem, behaviour of dimensions of fibres, descent for <ACCENT_0001>tale morphisms, etc,
etc. Before reading this section it may be a good idea to take a look at
the algebra results in Algebra, Section <REF_0001>.

<STRUCT_0002><STRUCT_0003>
Recall that a finite type ring map <MATH_0001> is quasi-finite at
a prime <MATH_0002> if <MATH_0003> defines an isolated point
of its fibre, see Algebra, Definition <REF_0002>.

<LOCKED_0001>
Let <MATH_0001> be a morphism of schemes.
<STRUCT_0001>
<STRUCT_0002> We say that <MATH_0002> is <TEXTITOPEN_0001>quasi-finite at a point <MATH_0003><TEXTITCLOSE_0001>
if there exist an affine neighbourhood <MATH_0004>
of <MATH_0005> and an affine open <MATH_0006> such that
<MATH_0007>, the ring map <MATH_0008> is of finite type,
and <MATH_0009> is quasi-finite at the prime of <MATH_0010> corresponding to <MATH_0011>
(see above).
<STRUCT_0003> We say <MATH_0012> is <TEXTITOPEN_0002>locally quasi-finite<TEXTITCLOSE_0002> if <MATH_0013> is
quasi-finite at every point <MATH_0014> of <MATH_0015>.
<STRUCT_0004> We say that <MATH_0016> is <TEXTITOPEN_0003>quasi-finite<TEXTITCLOSE_0003> if <MATH_0017> is of finite type
and every point <MATH_0018> is an isolated point of its fibre.
